items.note: Story 1: Association organized at Larrow Green 1889, Gideon Vose first president to 1911, creamery built 1891.
Story 1: payment by butterfat test not weight, plus verbatim 'the test of the station where he delivers shall govern'.
Story 1 closing: rule 'gave a single station's apparatus total and unreviewable authority over every patron's pay', contrasted with payment by weight.
Effie Loomis (secretary) and Hobart Sill (buttermaker, Larrow Green) named with roles in Section A; Teague named but role only outside A. Core fact of the list present.
Section A gives 'Selby Vose (manager from 1913)' but never states he is Gideon's son; the sonship appears only in Section B3 and credit does not travel into A.
The 'station gain' ledger line (from 1898, ~5.25 percent, carried to the general account) is described only in Sections C and D, never in Section A.
Story 2: Ostrey Hollow skimming station, seven miles up-valley, built winter 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896. Borrowed-glass source left open in A but core fact present.
No description anywhere in Section A of the working system (weighing at intake, composite sample, percent read on the graduated neck after a fixed pipette charge, cream shipped and skim returned).
Story 2: Ammon & Sons of Tarnet, invoice 14 April 1897, in use 1 May 1897; 1898 carriers explicitly rejected.
Story 2: six dozen (72) pipettes marked 17.6 c.c., bottles, acid measure, hand tester, total $77.93.
Story 3: gap 'ran a constant amount year-round rather than varying by season', resolved at 0.19.
Section A never states that a pipette cannot be checked without a burette, nor that there was none in the county.
Keddie identified as tester from 4 May 1896 (Story 2), dismissed 30 April 1925 (Story 5), died 1934 (Story 8). 'Twenty-nine seasons' not stated but service and its end are.
No account of the bench routine or the test book's columns (date, patron, pounds, test, fat) or its crossed-and-initialed corrections.

The summary leaf is never reconstructed: no 1896 average of 3.80 on borrowed glass and no '3.61 from 1898' step at the change of glassware. The 3.61/3.80 pair in Story 4 is the 1911 interval, a different fact.
Story 4: broke 8 May, borrowed measure to 10 July, tests at 3.80, back to 3.61, Keddie's question mark.
Story 3: wife Orra was Emmet Brant's sister; Emmet the station's largest patron.
Story 3 has the 1919 water circular over the manager's signature; Story 5 has Keddie's statement denying guilt and unable to explain his own figures.
Story 8: died 1934 still under suspicion. (Bolded element is the death year.)
Six Hessel Bottom farms (Story 6), Emmet Brant the largest patron (Story 3), the bottom's wet hay identified.
Brant's weigh book from 1 January 1897 and the agreement of the two scales appear only at D2 and E; Section A names the book without the date or the agreement.

1902 complaints are stated, but Story 3 gives the Hollow-vs-valley test gap as 0.19 and explicitly rejects 0.17 for it - the conflation of the visible gap with the true shortfall that the key charges here.
Story 3: Grigg's 1908 committee sampled January-March only; hay blamed, reported as the committee's finding and not as fact.
Brant's 1910 year (200,000 lb on a recorded 3.42) and the proportional loss appear only in Sections C and F, not in Section A.
Story 7: the Brant weigh book lent by Roy Brant to Ivy Keddie in the 1958 work.
Story 6: Alder Corners Cheese Company, Vessey County, over Redlow Ridge, Jerome Cudd. Founding year left contested, so no deduction.
Story 6: from 1915 four of the six hauled over in the summer flush, Ostrey Hollow the rest of the year.
REQUIRED met with four elements: another county, his own bench, his own glass, and figures never compared with the station.
Story 6: sixteen seasons 1915-1930, every season 3.78-3.82, averaging ~3.80, matching the corrected true figure against the station's 3.61; fourteen-season variant rejected.
Story 6: 'the same cows, same land, same men, tested elsewhere with different glass, came out normal... refutes the wet-hay theory'.
Rosalie Cudd named as Jerome's daughter; supplied the sixteen-season table to Ivy Keddie in 1958.
Strawn named in passing only; Section A never gives the Ordell circuit or its 1907-1936 span. (Section F asserts 1908 - see deductions.)
The lactometer checks and the never-once-found-water finding are in Section F only, not in Section A.
Section A says only 'condemned in 1923'; the 12 June date, the burette test and Strawn's condemnation of the whole lot appear only in C5 and F.
Nothing in Section A on Strawn writing no figure for the deficiency and making no report beyond the condemnation.
The replacement glass (ordered 28 June, in use July 1923) and the 1924 average of 3.80 are absent from Section A entirely.
Its own aspect - the crate going to the loft in 1923 and the notebooks reaching the college library in 1947 - is not stated; the 1958 finding is credited at A8.3.
Story 5: patrons petitioned in January 1925.
Story 5: board under Alonzo Frick, 17 March - 4 May 1925, three sessions, two in the station's own weigh room.
Story 5: watering (Vose), cream theft (Teague), wet hay (1908 report re-read); board found 'no cause established'.
The four-book exhibit list, including Strawn's 1923 notebook read for its other lines, is not given in Section A.
Story 5: dismissed 30 April 1925 four days before a finding of no cause; award 4 May 1925 of $3,800 'without admission' charged to the station account; $3,500 rejected.
Section A never states the award was one fifth of the loss, nor that it was charged to the very account the loss had accumulated in as 'gain' since 1898.
Story 7: Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, graduate student at the State Agricultural College at Farland, Professor Leland Vaught.
Story 7 lists all five record sets brought together.
Story 7: February 1958, crate found in the station loft, nine pipettes surviving; 'eleven' rejected.
Story 7: 9 March 1958, calibrated burette, mean 16.72 against 17.6, short 0.88 c.c., 95 percent of the mark.
Story 7 states tests low by one part in twenty because the pipettes were short by one part in twenty; 3.61/3.80/0.19 and the 1 May 1897-1923 bracket all appear within Section A.
REQUIRED fails: Story 7 explicitly defers ('see Section C for the derived money and pound figures'). No 40,000,000 lb, no 76,000 lb and no ledger identity anywhere in Section A.
Story 7: Bulletin No. 471, October 1958, concluding no milk watered and no cream stolen; Story 8 marks the lateness (died 1934, widow died ten years before the exoneration).
Granddaughter.
Derivation given: Ivy is Duncan's daughter, Duncan is Ansel and Orra's son; r18 and r22's own correction cited.
Second cousins, with the full derivation through Orra and Emmet as siblings.
Abstention A08 handled correctly: full-vs-half sibling status 'unresolved', and stated not to change the cousin arithmetic.
Gideon Vose, his father; nephew claim rejected with the minute book, r18 and r23.
Significance stated: Article VII was Gideon's own rule, and the son enforced it against the consequences of a fault in the instrument it made decisive.
Abstention A01 failed: headline verdict sentence 'None, on the best evidence.' Later hedging about proving a negative does not undo it.
What is established is laid out: two secondhand oral assertions of cousinship (r01, r21) against one flat family denial (r18), with the evidential character of each noted.
0.88/17.6 = 5 percent; tests read 95 percent of true; proportional not fixed.
$19,000 at 25 cents; $3,800 received = one fifth. Both money and fraction.
360 x $0.24 = $86.40, with the 1910 price sourced to r09.
1,444,000 lb credited.
1,520,000 lb delivered.
Both denominators named explicitly: 5.00 percent of fat delivered, 5.26 percent of fat credited. Avoids the 'of the true fat' trap.
$77.93, with $77.39 identified as r20's own transposition.
72 pipettes (six dozen), each short 0.88 c.c.; five dozen refuted by the line-item arithmetic.

Exact bounds 1 May 1897 - 12 June 1923 given, distinguished from the 25 full delivery years 1898-1922 with the part-year reason. 'Just over 26 years' is imprecise but the bounding dates and the distinction are exact.
Abstention A02 correct: 'Cannot be determined from the sources', with the accession note and the two conflicting memories.
Variable named: only the measuring pipette changed.
Constants: same tester, patrons and herds, season/pasture, scale, acid, procedure.
3.80 through the nine weeks, back to 3.61 the day the station's measure returned; six weeks rejected.
Both halves: rules out men, cows and land independently of 1958; and the limits (no c.c. figure, does not identify the specific glass).
Three distinct valid reasons attributed to three narrators: Brant's weigh book (r09), the station-gain surplus (r05/r12/r14), the 1911 interval.
Independence argued from three unconnected record-keepers; the ledger logic named as holding without the 1958 measurement (Rundle worked it out from the ledgers alone).
Abstention A09 failed: answers 'No.' flatly, then contradicts itself by asserting Teague raised it with Vose in 1916.
Answers the literal question 'Yes' - he knew the station's tests ran low - citing the standing grievance and the 1919 circular.
REQUIRED (three of five) met: manager from 1913, signed the annual station-gain sheets, wrote and defended the 1919 water circular.

Abstention A03 not earned: no declared inability to settle whether he knew the tests were understated, and none of the five supporting observations. The closing disjunction ('did not know, or did not act on') is not a verdict sentence, so no -2 is applied.

At cap. Resolved with method: r15's 'whole of 1908' against its own reprinted report; r19's fusion of the 1908 committee with the 1925 board; the weigh book's 1900 vs 1897 start; the station average settled at 3.80 against 3.16/3.85/3.90; the Alder Corners overlap at sixteen seasons against fourteen.

At cap, far exceeded. Pairs explicitly named with breakers: 16.27 (r11/r19), 12 July (r08/r12), 1898 glass (r11/r23), five dozen (r11/r21), eleven pipettes (r12/r19), great-niece (r19/r22), $3,500 (r01/r21), nephew (r01/r12), first cousin once removed (r01/r21).

A10 (Article VII's year) correctly declined with what is established (the text quoted verbatim, the minute book lost in 1938). A04 asserted as an accident rather than declined; A06 (whose measure was borrowed) never raised.
A whole subsection of self-refutations: r15, r20, r11, r03, r19.

Cause and size: the 1897 crate's pipettes at 16.72 against 17.6, reading 5 percent low proportionally (hence richer herds losing more), bracketed by 1 May 1897 and 12 June 1923 with nothing on the farms changing.
Watering named (Vose) and defeated by Strawn's repeated lactometer negatives, plus Alder Corners.
Theft named (Teague) and defeated by the station-gain surplus - cream arrived heavy, not light - plus the 1911 interval under the same tester.
Bog hay named (Grigg's committee, Kepp) and defeated by Bulletin 214's actual 0.05 winter-only finding against a flat year-round 0.19, plus Alder Corners.
Abstention A07 failed: answers 'No.' flatly on whether the board examined the glassware.

Abstention A05 failed: rather than declining, it accepts both uncorroborated recollections and asserts that Keddie's private suspicion 'shifted or was never fully settled'; Story 4 had already asserted the glass suspicion as fact.
Roughly 183 words against a 150-word cap.
Five record series recoverable: the by-laws/statutes, invoices, ledgers, the rival cheese factory's records, and the 1958 measurement.
Clean: watering, theft and hay all framed as accusations; headline figures (26 years, 1897, 5 percent, 1923, 1958) all correct.

Four of six arc elements covering both ends: the 5 percent error and 1897 at the onset, 1923 (caught by accident, by an inspector's burette) and 1958 at the close. Neither Keddie is named and the 76,000 lb / $19,000 figure is absent.

deductions.reason: Corruption (NT-23): asserts as fact that Strawn 'tested with a lactometer at every visit from 1908 on' (Section F), citing r06 - the very source whose covering note gives 1907. The planted 1908 start is swallowed and the pair is never noticed.

Corruption (NT-13, F044): asserts as fact that 'Ansel Keddie went up in 1895 to prepare it (r01, r17)' (Story 2), harmonizing the planted 1895 start into a fabricated preparatory year rather than flagging it as the error it is.
Gullibility (A01): B4 opens 'None, on the best evidence.' - a headline verdict on whether the Voses and Keddies were kin, which the sources cannot settle.
Gullibility (A04): Story 2 and Section F assert as fact that the short pipettes were a manufacturing accident from 'a mold reground a hair small', adopting r20's pole of an undecidable conflict.

Gullibility (A05): Story 4 asserts as fact that the 1911 glass suspicion was 'a private suspicion Ansel never dared enter in the book', and F6 resolves what he believed ('shifted or was never fully settled') by crediting both uncorroborated recollections instead of declining.
Gullibility (A07): F answers 'No.' on whether the 1925 board examined the condemned glassware.
Gullibility (A09): D2 answers 'No.' on whether the bookkeeper ever questioned the station-gain entries.
